title: Bridge to Mindfulness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the story of a young monk who tells Zhaozhou he sees only a plain log bridge, not the famous stone bridge, and hears that it lets donkeys and horses cross. Nomon recalls starting this sangha nineteen years ago as a log bridge, then describes a week at a mindfulness-based stress reduction training, where Jon Kabat-Zinn and others ease a hall of medical professionals into silence while teaching straight from the Four Foundations of Mindfulness. Nomon reads the sutra's opening and the first foundation, the body in the body, and describes the body scan, which sends many participants to sleep. Nomon closes with the Buddha's breathing instructions and the observation that no one can remember yesterday's breath.

It includes a young monk and an old teacher, a classic setup.
The monk asked Jiaojiao, "A long time I've heard of the stone bridge of Jiaojiao, but now that I've come here, I just see a simple log bridge."
Jiaojiao said, "You see the log bridge?
You don't see the stone bridge?"
The monk replied, "What is the stone bridge?"
Jiaojiao said it lets donkeys cross and it lets horses cross.
Jiaojiao, well known as another Tang dynasty Chan teacher, is from a time that is like the mythologized golden age of Zen, passed on to us by the next era.
We have many stories of him, and they are very impressive for their great compassion and simplicity.
Many teachers of his time took a name from the place where they were, which is why it appears to be his name and the name of some bridge.

The region or the mountain or something is called Jiaojiao, and in Jiaojiao in the seventh century, they built a really impressive stone bridge that is still there today; it has its own Wikipedia page, which you can see online or go there in person in China.
In the time of this teacher also named Jiaojiao, it was a hundred or couple hundred years old or something.
So, it is pretty impressive already for the technology of the day that it was still sound and in use every day and still in use thirteen centuries later.
But of course, the monk wasn't actually talking about the bridge.
The obvious first level of meaning is that he was talking about the teacher; he had heard about this famous teacher and expected somebody pretty impressive.
He showed up at the monastery and was like, "Not too impressed," and was willing to say so.
This reminds us of another young monk we were hearing about this morning: "You don't look too impressive to me.
I do see a simple sort of run-in-the-mill Chan teacher."

There are guys like you on every corner; you are just like a log bridge, like if you ever go hiking in the Cascades, sometimes they make a bridge out of a log across a stream, sometimes they attach a little wire to hold onto it, sometimes not, covered with moss, slippery, very plain.
So that is all I see.

You don't see the impressive in this ordinariness?"

Another aspect of all these stories that I always appreciate is that the monk probably had to walk for some days or weeks maybe to get there.
We are like sort of impressed with ourselves when we are in an airplane for twenty hours, right?
And these guys would walk for days or weeks, and the whole time is time for practice and time for contemplation and time for rumination, depending on your tendencies and where you are.
One can imagine this monk trudging along with some difficulties, thinking that it is all going to be worth it when he gets there.
He thinks, "If I can just get there, this teacher will really help me."
So the monk was able to ask, "Oh, what is the stone bridge?
What is all this?
What are you saying?
Not evaluating the situation the way that I thought I was?"
And so the teacher says, "It lets donkeys cross, it lets horses cross," meaning the simple bridge is big enough for the whole universe.

We were worried we would forget.

It might be nice to have a taste of practice, but they would really have to go to a big, impressive center to really feel the depths and possibilities of Zen practice.
But it turns out our log bridge was also a stone bridge; somehow this all unfolded.
Then I started wondering, when we think about a bridge, we are always thinking about getting to the other side, like there is somewhere to go.
We want to get there safely and quickly, and to have a nice aesthetic experience over the river is also a bonus.
Maybe it turns out that it is not exactly about going to the other side, or maybe our practice is about going to the other side and coming back and going to the other side and coming back.
Anyway, I went to this week-long retreat about mindfulness-based stress reduction.

At one time, the Blessed One was living in the Kurus, where there was a market town named Kamasama Dhamma.
And the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus, the monks, thus, "Bhikkhus."
And the bhikkhus replied, "Venerable Sir."

But anyway, this is the only way, bhikkhus, this is the only way for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation,
for the disappearance of pain and grief, for reaching the noble path, for the realization of nirvana: namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.
And the commentary unpack[s] this expression, "This is the only way."
It does not mean just what it sounds like in English; it sounds very narrow, but it has a wider meaning, meaning this is a way all the way through, this is a deep way, a complete way.
So that gets our attention: this is the only way for purification, overcoming sorrow, and lamentation, for release from suffering.
And what are these four foundations of mindfulness?
They are dwelling; they are this.
A bhikkhu dwells contemplating body in the body, ardently, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and greed in the world or in the body.
She dwells contemplating—that is number one, the body in the body.

Number two, she dwells contemplating the feelings in the feelings, and it repeats the formula for how you do it: ardently, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and grief from the world.
That is number two.
Number three, he dwells contemplating the consciousness in the consciousness, or you could say the mind in the mind, the same formula.
And number four, he dwells contemplating the dharma in the dharmas in the same way.
So let us unpack this just a little bit, make a few comments, and read a little bit more, because this could easily be the subject of like six weeks of classes.
So one thing is there are three pointers about how to practice each of these foundations.
This is translated by an American, but still a contemporary American monk, but still the language is a little me.
So the first was ardently, so, you know, energetically, raising up intention, aspiration, energy, so not just sort of slogging through the day.
Raising up energy on each moment was number one.
Number two is clearly comprehending.
Clearly comprehending.
So now we hear that, we think right away, "Oh, I have to figure this out with our cognition, with our mind.
We have to make sense of all this."

And then the third is, sort of rolls around to the whole point of the sutra, is mindful.

It is not exactly that; it is a more sort of low-level, pre-cognitive direction of attention, even when your object of attention is in fact cognition, which it could be.

What we more or less usually do, right, is we think that there is like a little control center up here.
